title: Whose AI Will Rule The World? | NOEMA
gist: Shanghai-based editor Jacob Dreyer argues China's AI and quantum push is a civilizational continuation — state-directed, sacrifice-tolerant, exported to the Global South — while Trump science adviser Michael Kratsios is quietly restructuring U.S. science along Chinese lines, substituting AI for the millions of STEM graduates America lacks.

insights.claim: China funds elite scientists by transferring large sums directly into their jurisdiction rather than through competitive grant cycles, giving individuals like quantum physicist Pan Jianwei blank-check operational authority under Xi Jinping's 'sci-tech self-reliance' mandate.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Capital allocation speed, not aggregate R&D dollars, is China's edge in deep tech; expect faster commercialization cycles in quantum, materials and batteries than Western peer-reviewed systems can match.
insights.quote: Pan just gets large sums of money transferred into his jurisdiction.
insights.locator: The Scientific Sovereign

insights.claim: China Telecom acquired a 23% stake in QuantumCTek, a firm founded by Pan Jianwei's academic research team, to build national quantum communications infrastructure on Pan's proprietary hardware.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: State-owned carriers are the anchor customers and equity backers for Chinese quantum hardware — a template for how Chinese frontier tech reaches revenue without venture markets.
insights.quote: China Telecom acquired a 23% stake in the firm to build out unhackable national communications infrastructure based directly on Pan’s proprietary hardware.
insights.locator: His work and influence extend far beyond university walls

insights.claim: Pan Jianwei is not a Communist Party member — he belongs to the Jiusan Society, one of China's eight legally sanctioned parties — and has stayed in his Hefei lab rather than taking an administrative post, which the author argues is now the more powerful position.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Watch the rise of a technocratic class in China that is politically untouchable without being Party-embedded — a new node of influence for anyone mapping Chinese industrial policy.
insights.locator: Although he is increasingly prominent in China’s political ecosystem

insights.claim: Beijing's stated causal chain is that technological change creates economic change which creates political change, and it believes a revolution is underway across AI, quantum computing, biotech, new energy, and materials science simultaneously.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Chinese policy treats these five fields as one integrated program, so capital and talent flow across them together — sector-by-sector analysis of Chinese tech will understate the coordination.
insights.locator: In an email to me, Pan shared five pages of thoughts

insights.claim: Pan Jianwei, who co-authored the first experimental demonstration of quantum teleportation in 1997 under 2022 Nobel laureate Anton Zeilinger, is widely seen as one of China's most likely Nobel candidates.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Credentials matter for soft-power signaling: a Chinese physics Nobel would reframe the 'China only copies' narrative that underpins some Western complacency.
insights.locator: For the past few months, I’ve been corresponding with Pan Jianwei

insights.claim: The 2025 U.S. National Security Strategy names quantum alongside AI and biotech as a field the U.S. must not cede to China, and the White House has been publicly invoking quantum supremacy.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Quantum has moved from research curiosity to declared national-security priority — a leading indicator for defense-adjacent quantum and post-quantum-cryptography budgets.
insights.locator: In recent months, the White House has been tweeting about quantum supremacy

insights.claim: The strategic stake in quantum computing is encryption: a Chinese breakthrough would provide a way around traditional public-key encryption and let Beijing read American secrets.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Frames the migration to post-quantum cryptography as a policy-forced spend, not an optional upgrade, across government and financial infrastructure.
insights.quote: if China breaks through on quantum computing, it’ll have a way around traditional public-key encryption and be able to read all of America’s secrets.
insights.locator: It’s seen as important because

insights.claim: Quantum computing differs from classical computing the way Chinese characters differ from the Roman alphabet — same function, radically different mechanism — because qubits exploit superposition and entanglement to map entire solution spaces at once rather than stepping through them.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: A usable mental model for judging which workloads quantum actually threatens — combinatorial search and cryptography, not general compute.
insights.quote: In this sense, quantum computing is to computing what Chinese characters are to the Roman alphabet: Both apparently fulfill the same function, but the way in which they do so is radically different.
insights.locator: By manipulating these fluid probabilities

themes.theme: Washington quietly copying Beijing's science model

insights.claim: Trump science adviser Michael Kratsios's science-policy report — pitched as the biggest revision since Vannevar Bush's 'Science: The Endless Frontier' — is a concrete shift from decentralized academic inquiry toward a centralized, mission-driven, state-backed system that mirrors Beijing's tech-governance model.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: U.S. science funding is being restructured toward directed national missions; position for concentrated, politically-selected winners rather than broad university-grant beneficiaries.
insights.quote: a fundamental shift away from the traditional, decentralized Western model of free academic inquiry toward a centralized, mission-driven, state-backed system that mirrors Beijing’s tech-governance model.
insights.locator: A New Golden Age?

insights.claim: The Kratsios report attacks consensus-driven peer review as sluggish and conservative and proposes 'golden tickets' that let individual state-appointed reviewers unilaterally fund high-risk proposals without consensus approval.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Discretionary single-reviewer funding turns U.S. science grants into something closer to a venture portfolio — expect higher variance, faster deployment, and more political capture risk.
insights.locator: For example, echoing a long-time Thiel idea

insights.claim: The centerpieces of U.S. science reform are the 'Genesis Mission' and an NSF initiative called 'X-Labs,' explicitly structured as Manhattan Project-style multidisciplinary organizations applying AI to accelerate scientific productivity while bypassing legacy academic boundaries.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Named programs to track for contract flow: AI-for-science compute, instrumentation and lab-automation vendors are the direct beneficiaries.
insights.locator: The centerpieces of the Kratsios report

insights.claim: The U.S. cannot replicate China's key scientific input — millions of STEM graduates — so the American strategy is effectively to substitute AI, Dario Amodei's 'country of geniuses in a datacenter,' for Chinese human scale.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: The entire U.S. science-competitiveness bet now rests on AI research productivity delivering; if it underdelivers, the scale gap reasserts itself and the compute buildout loses its policy justification.
insights.quote: But even if the U.S. adopts many Chinese methods, it lacks the critical ingredient of Chinese science success: Chinese people. Lots of them.
insights.locator: But even if the U.S. adopts many Chinese methods

insights.claim: Dan Wang and Julian Gewirtz have argued in The New York Times that the Pentagon's proactive supervision of Anthropic is a direct copy of Chinese state capitalism, while Rep. Zoe Lofgren says the administration has been systematically destroying the U.S. science enterprise.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: State entanglement with frontier AI labs is becoming an explicit political fight — a governance risk factor for private AI valuations and for lab independence.
insights.locator: Democratic critics (like Rep. Zoe Lofgren of California)

insights.claim: Beijing's method is not nationalizing tech firms but integrating the state into private enterprises, and the tight coupling of policymakers, fundamental research, emerging fields like batteries, and supply-chain dominance is what makes the model work.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Predicting Chinese sector dominance means tracking where state research funding and supply-chain policy converge — batteries and materials are the current live example.
insights.quote: Beijing doesn’t nationalize tech firms; it integrates the state into private enterprises.
insights.locator: Beijing doesn’t nationalize tech firms

themes.theme: China's AI export machine to the Global South

insights.claim: China runs a China-ASEAN Artificial Intelligence Application Cooperation Center in Nanning, Guangxi, that showcases AI applications in agriculture, logistics, public safety, manufacturing, local finance, healthcare and education to leaders from Vietnam, Laos and Indonesia.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Chinese AI is being sold as a vertical governance stack to emerging markets, not as raw models — the addressable market for Chinese AI is state procurement across the Global South.
insights.locator: When AI Runs The World

insights.claim: Nanning's nominal GDP per capita is nearly $10,000 — roughly double Vietnam's and nearly five times Laos's or Cambodia's — which makes a second-tier Chinese city itself the sales demo for Chinese-style development.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: The income gap between inland China and ASEAN neighbors is the actual pitch; it also implies Chinese firms have a cost-appropriate product for these markets that Western vendors lack.
insights.quote: Nanning’s nominal GDP per capita sits at nearly $10,000, double Vietnam’s and nearly five times higher than in Laos or Cambodia.
insights.locator: Nanning itself felt like a display

insights.claim: China's five-year plans assign distinct roles by region — Beijing and Shanghai for capital-heavy innovation and research, Guangxi for disseminating it to Southeast Asia — making regional specialization a deliberate export architecture.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Geographic policy mandates tell you where Chinese capex lands next; border provinces are the distribution layer for tech exports.
insights.locator: The Chinese five-year plans allocate different tasks

insights.claim: China's 'AI+' plan targets sectors where the state already has a role and where the population cannot afford market-priced services — cutting electricity costs, securing food supply, delivering AI-driven national healthcare — treating AI as a commodity like electricity rather than a product.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Implies Chinese AI monetizes through utility-like deployment and state budgets, not subscription software margins — a different comp set entirely from U.S. AI firms.
insights.quote: AI is understood as a tool, or perhaps a commodity like electricity, and the Chinese plan is to use that tool to solve Chinese problems
insights.locator: The Chinese government’s AI+ plan

insights.claim: Chinese AI policy operates from an explicit problem list that AI is systematically applied to, and the resulting solutions are exported to whoever will take them — increasingly the Global South.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Chinese AI diffusion is a policy output, not a market outcome — expect standards and platform lock-in in emerging markets ahead of any Western commercial response.
insights.quote: There is a list of problems and AI is being used systematically to solve those problems.
insights.locator: The Chinese AI policy that American policymakers

insights.claim: Chinese tech companies are expected to symbolically pledge allegiance to national heritage — the author saw an ancient Chinese scroll painting displayed under a CamScanner screen at the World AI Conference in Shanghai.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Civilizational branding is now a compliance cost for Chinese AI firms — a tell for which companies are politically secure and which are still proving loyalty.
insights.locator: At the recent World AI Conference in Shanghai

insights.claim: Thiel's 2014 'Zero to One' framework cast China as definite pessimism (planning against expected disaster) and 1950s America as definite optimism (planning because the future is bright), but as AI changes everything the Chinese now appear more optimistic than the Americans.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: A sentiment inversion that shows up in risk appetite: Chinese capital and policy lean into AI buildout while U.S. discourse leans defensive — relevant to relative equity risk premia in the two tech complexes.
insights.quote: if anything, as AI changes everything, the Chinese seem more optimistic than the Americans.
insights.locator: In 2014, Thiel wrote in his tech-founder bible

insights.claim: China today resembles the mid-century United States: an industrial superpower that senses it is not quite as sophisticated as the decadent power it wishes to replace.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: If the analogy holds, China's status anxiety drives aggressive talent absorption and prestige science spending — a decades-long, not cyclical, capital commitment.
insights.quote: China today resembles the U.S. then: an industrial superpower that senses it is not quite as sophisticated as the decadent power it wishes to replace.
insights.locator: The Silicon Valley radicals adjacent to Thiel

insights.claim: Key parts of the Chinese model are non-transferable to the U.S. for cultural reasons — surveillance being the clearest case, as the backlash to Flock demonstrates — so American adoption will be partial and contested.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Surveillance-adjacent AI has a structurally lower U.S. TAM than China's; domestic political backlash is a real revenue ceiling for that category.
insights.locator: Many aspects of the Chinese model would not fly in America.

themes.theme: Writing systems as civilizational source code

insights.claim: Algorithmic consciousness is unusually compatible with the traditional Chinese civilizational source code, because a script built on the optimized visual juxtaposition of interlocking patterns maps naturally onto neural networks and onto an individual embedded in a larger network of thought.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: A cultural-fit argument for faster Chinese societal adoption of AI — adoption friction, not model quality, may be the decisive variable in the AI race.
insights.quote: A civilization whose thinking has always been about the optimized, visual juxtaposition of concepts finds its ultimate realization in the neural network.
insights.locator: Today, the dominant mechanism by which information is transmitted

insights.claim: China's five-year plans function like Shang-dynasty oracle bones: not economic forecasts but state-directed inscriptions designed to conjure a reality into existence.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Read Chinese plan targets as commitment devices that mobilize resources rather than as predictions to be scored — the mobilization itself is the tradable signal.
insights.quote: Like today’s five-year plans, the oracle bones were not economic forecasts; they were magical, state-directed inscriptions designed to conjure a reality into existence.
insights.locator: And yet, much as the story of Adam and Eve

insights.claim: The right analogy for AI is not fire or electricity but the invention of writing — a system that simultaneously liberates thought and constrains it — implying AI will shape what its users can think, not merely what they can do.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: If AI is infrastructure for cognition, whoever sets the defaults captures durable, path-dependent influence — argues for valuing distribution and standards over model benchmarks.
insights.quote: But a more apt analogy might be the invention of writing: a system that both liberates our thoughts — and constrains them.
insights.locator: SHANGHAI — Today, China and the United States

insights.claim: The questions humanity currently asks AI may be as trivial as the Shang asking oracle bones where to hunt, but the platform built to answer them may birth systems and ideas nobody can currently imagine — an argument that today's mundane AI use cases understate the eventual payoff.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: A patience argument against dismissing AI on current-use-case ROI; the infrastructure thesis outlives the application disappointment.
insights.quote: The AI being built is not a good in itself; the questions we ask it may be as trivial as the Shang asking the oracle bones what part of the forest was a good place to hunt.
